# First steps with Markdown {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## What is Markdown?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [A simple markup language]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

- A lightweight "**markup language**" in which you write in plain-text,
  adding simple formatting instructions using visible characters.

. . .

- This plain-text **source** Markdown file can be converted into various output
  formats, like HTML or PDF.

. . .

- This process of conversion is called "**rendering**",
  during which the formatting instructions are applied
  (and the visible characters are removed).

:::
::: {.column width="5%"}
<div style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

. . .

### [A first example]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Surrounding text with single or double asterisks (**`*`**) applies
*italic* and **bold** formatting, respectively:

- \*italic example\* produces *italic example*
- \*\*bold example\*\* produces **bold example**

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
We refer to these constructs (* for italic, etc.) as the "syntax" of the language.
:::

:::
:::

## Markdown in VS Code

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="70%"}

Markdown files have extension `.md`,
and when you save a file with that extension in VS Code:

- Some formatting is automatically applied in the editor.
- You can open a live **Preview** of the rendered version, using the
  icon on the right.

. . .

:::
::: {.column width="30%"}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

![](../img/markdown-preview-vscode.png){fig-align="center" width="40%" fig-alt="A screenshot of the Markdown preview icon in VS Code."}

:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

## Why use Markdown? It is:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%" .box-blue}
### Easy to use

- **Easy to write**:
  you only need to know a dozen or so syntax constructs to get started.

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
- **Easy to read** in source form
  (and VS Code applies some formatting even there).
:::

:::
::: {.column width="3%"}
:::
::: {.column width="30%" .box-amber .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}
### Very widely used

- The standard for documentation in computational fields.

- Has become even more well-known with the rise of GenAI,
  which prefers to read and write with Markdown (e.g., `CLAUDE.md`).

:::

::: {.column width="3%"}
:::

::: {.column width="30%" .box-teal .fragment data-fragment-index="3"}
### Powerful and versatile

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="4"}
- One source file can be converted to many output formats.
:::

::: {.fragment data-fragment-index="5"}
- Markdown extensions enable:
  
  - Executable code in documents,
    such as in [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) (covered in week 13)

  - Creating slides (such as these!) and websites (such as this one!)
:::

:::
:::

# The most common Markdown syntax {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Headers

To create headers, use one or more `#` characters, followed by a space:

```
# Intro to Markdown

## Section 1: The basics
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- One `#` makes a level-1 header (largest --- use only for document titles)
- Two `##` makes a level-2 header, and so forth for smaller headers

[TODO - add screenshot]{.todo}

## Lists

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

**Type:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```{.markdown code-line-numbers="false"}
- Pine Warbler
- Palm Warbler
```

:::
::: {.column width="7%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}

**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

- Pine Warbler
- Palm Warbler

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```{.markdown code-line-numbers="false"}
1. Swamp Sparrow
2. Tree Sparrow
2. Field Sparrow
```

:::
::: {.column width="7%"}
:::
::: {.column width="47%"}

1. Swamp Sparrow
2. Tree Sparrow
2. Field Sparrow

:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

<details class=details-quiz><summary>
Do you notice anything striking about the second example? _(Click to see the answer)_
</summary>

Even though the last two items are both numbered "2.",
they are rendered as "2." and "3." in the output.
Markdown automatically numbers ordered lists,
so you don't have to worry about numbering them correctly in the source.

</details>

## Overview of syntax so far

| Syntax/source           | Result/rendered output                                             |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| \*italic\*              | *italic* text (or usae an underscore: \_italic\_)                  |
| \*\*bold\*\*            | **bold** text                                                      |
| # My Title              | Header level 1 (largest)                                           |
| ## My Section           | Header level 2 (smaller)                                           |
| - List item             | Unordered (bulleted) list                                          |
| 1. List item            | Ordered (numbered) list                                            |

: {.hover .striped}

## Code formatting

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [What is code formatting]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Applying "code formatting" to text means that it...

- is displayed in a [monospaced font]{style="font-family:monospace; font-size:0.9em"},
  often with a different text and/or background color
- may have language-specific syntax highlighting.

:::
::: {.column width="5%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [How to apply it]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Surround text with backticks (\`), single backticks for inline code,
and triple backticks for code blocks. 

{{< fa user-edit >}} _Take a moment to find the backtick key on your keyboard_
_(usually above the Tab key)._

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="48%"}

**Type:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

The command \`date\` prints the current date and time.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

\`\`\`bash\
\# Print the current date and time\
date\
\`\`\`

:::
::: {.column width="4%"}
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

The command `date` prints the current date and time.

<br>

```{.bash code-line-numbers="false"}
# Print the current date and time
date
```

:::
:::

## Overview of code-formatting syntax

| Syntax/source                                  | Result/rendered output                              |
| ---------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| \`inline code\`                                | "Code-formatted" text for inline use: `inline code` |
| \`\`\`bash <br> code <br> ```` ``` ````        | `bash`-formatted language code block                |
| \`\`\`r <br> code <br> ```` ``` ````           | `r`-formatted language code block                   |
| ```` ``` ```` <br> code <br> ```` ``` ````     | Generic/language-agnostic code block                |
|                                                |                                                     |

: {.striped tbl-colwidths="[25,75]"}

## Overview of most common syntax

| Syntax/source           | Result/rendered output                                             |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| \*italic\*              | *italic* text (or usae an underscore: \_italic\_)                  |
| \*\*bold\*\*            | **bold** text                                                      |
| # My Title              | Header level 1 (largest)                                           |
| ## My Section           | Header level 2 (smaller)                                           |
| - List item             | Unordered (bulleted) list                                          |
| 1. List item            | Ordered (numbered) list                                            |
| \<https://website.com\> | Clickable link with visible URL: <https://website.com>             |
| \[link text\]\(url\)    | Clickable link with "hidden" URL: [link text](https://website.com) |
| \-\-\-                  | Horizontal rule (use 3+ dashes)                                    |
| \> Text                 | Blockquote (like quoted text in emails)                            |

: {.hover .striped}

# Whitespace in Markdown {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Leave whitespace around syntax elements

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [A blank line between sections]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Always leave a blank line between different sections,
such as lists, headers, and regular paragraphs
to guarantee that they are interpreted correctly.

```bash-in-nocolor
## Chapter 2: List of ...

- Item 1
- Item 2

For example, ....
```

:::
::: {.column width="5%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [A spaces after specific characters]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Always leave a space after heading (`#`) and list (`-`/`1.`)
characters, or they won't be interpreted correctly

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Type:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
##An important list

-x
-y
-z
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

##An important list

-x -y -z

:::
:::

:::
:::

. . .

<br>

<details class=details-quiz><summary>
Do you notice anything striking about the second example? _(Click to see the answer)_
</summary>

Not only were no bullet points used,
but the list items were collapsed into a single line.
What is that all about?

</details>

## Some whitespace is ignored or collapsed

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Type:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
Line 1.
Line 2.
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

Line 1.
Line 2.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**Instead, you'll have to start a new paragraph with a blank line between the**
**two lines of text:**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
Paragraph 1.

Paragraph 2.
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

Paragraph 1.

Paragraph 2.

:::
:::

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

**Multiple consecutive spaces or blank lines are "collapsed" into a single one:**

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
Empty             spaces

Many


blank lines
```

:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

Empty spaces

Many

blank lines

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

# Optional self-study material {background-color="#A7B1B7"}

## Creating tables

Creating tables in Markdown is a bit more tricky than other elements.
Use vertical bars `|` and dashes `-` like so:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Type:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />
<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

```
| city       | inhabitants |
|------------|-------------|
| Columbus   | 906 K       |
| Cleveland  | 368 K       |
```

:::
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}

**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />
<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

| city       | inhabitants |
|------------|-------------|
| Columbus   | 906 K       |
| Cleveland  | 368 K       |

:::
:::

## Inserting images/figures

Images can be inserted using the following syntax:

```
![Optional caption](image.jpg)
```

[TODO - finish]{.todo}

## Forcing a single linebreak

You can force a single **linebreak** (as opposed to a new paragraph) by adding
a backslash `\` after the last character on a line:

::: columns
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

**Type:**  

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
My first sentence.\
My second sentence.
```

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

My first sentence.\
My second sentence.

:::
:::

## Forcing additional space between paragraphs

We saw earlier that Markdown collapses multiple consecutive spaces or blank lines into a single one.
If you want to force additional space between paragraphs,
you'll have to resort to an HTML tag ---
each **`<br>`** item forces a visible linebreak:

::: columns
::: {.column width="10%"}
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}

**Type:**  

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />

```
One <br> word <br> per line
and <br> <br> <br> <br> <br>
several blank lines.
```

:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
**Rendered as:**

<hr style="width:95%; margin:0.3em 0;" />
 
One <br> word <br> per line
and <br> <br> <br> <br> <br>
several blank lines.

:::
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
You can use any HTML markup in Markdown!
Maybe not everyone's cup of tea,
but this is one way in which Markdown is very versatile.
:::
